title: Bitwise Operations
summary: See numbers in binary and use &, |, ^, ~, and shifts, including Java's unsigned >>> and common bit tricks.
intro: Every int is 32 bits, and Java lets you work on those bits directly. Bit operators power flags and permissions, fast multiplication by 2, and a few classic interview tricks. This lesson shows how to read and print binary, the four bit operators, the three shifts, bit masks, and the tricks people reach for most.

steps.title: Binary and the bit operators
steps.body:
Java writes binary literals with `0b`, and underscores keep them readable: `0b1010` is 10 and `0b1111_1111` is 255. `Integer.toBinaryString(x)` drops leading zeros, so pad a value from 0 to 255 to 8 digits with `String.format("%8s", ...)` and turn the spaces into zeros. `Integer.parseInt(s, 2)` goes the other way.

```java
String bits = String.format("%8s", Integer.toBinaryString(5)).replace(' ', '0'); // 00000101
int value = Integer.parseInt("1011", 2); // 11
```

The bit operators compare the two numbers one bit position at a time:

- `a & b` (AND) has a 1 where both bits are 1.
- `a | b` (OR) has a 1 where either bit is 1.
- `a ^ b` (XOR) has a 1 where exactly one bit is 1.
- `~a` (NOT) flips all 32 bits, so `~13` is negative. Mask with `& 0b1111_1111` to keep only the low 8 bits.

`&` and `|` also work on booleans, but they never short-circuit: both sides always run, so `s != null & s.isEmpty()` still calls `isEmpty` on a null `s`. Keep `&&` and `||` for conditions.

Gotcha: `==` binds tighter than `&`, so `n & 1 == 0` is a compile error. Write `(n & 1) == 0` to test for even.

example.title: Two bytes side by side
example.prompt: Read two ints and a binary String, show both ints in 8-bit binary, combine them with AND, OR, and XOR, flip the first with NOT, test each for odd, and convert the String to decimal.
example.explanation: `bin8` pads `Integer.toBinaryString` to 8 digits so the columns line up and you can check each operator bit by bit: 1101 & 1010 keeps only the shared 1000. `~a` flips all 32 bits, so `& LOW_BYTE` (written as the literal `0b1111_1111`) keeps just the low 8. The odd test wraps `a & 1` in parentheses before comparing with `==`, and unlike `a % 2 == 1` it also works for negative odd numbers. `Integer.parseInt(bits, 2)` reads the String as base 2.

practice.title: AND, OR, XOR table
practice.prompt:
Read two ints and a binary String, then print their AND, OR, and XOR and the value of the String.

1. Finish `bin8` so it returns `x` as exactly 8 binary digits, padded with leading zeros.
2. Print `AND: `, `OR: `, and `XOR: ` lines, each followed by the decimal result, a space, and its 8-bit binary.
3. Print `Value: ` followed by the decimal value of the binary String.

Input:

```text
12 10
10011
```

Expected output:

```text
AND: 8 00001000
OR: 14 00001110
XOR: 6 00000110
Value: 19
```
hints: `Integer.toBinaryString` drops leading zeros. Format it into a field 8 wide with `%8s`, then swap the spaces for zeros.
Use `printf` with `%d %s%n` and pass `a & b` and `bin8(a & b)`.

steps.title: Shifts and negative numbers
steps.body:
`n << k` moves every bit k places left and fills with zeros, which multiplies by 2 to the k (until it overflows). Right shifts come in two kinds:

- `n >> k` (arithmetic) copies the sign bit in, so a negative stays negative.
- `n >>> k` (unsigned) fills with zeros, so for any k from 1 to 31 a negative turns positive.

Java ints use two's complement: `-x` is stored as `~x + 1`. That is why `~x` equals `-x - 1` and `Integer.toBinaryString(-1)` is 32 ones.

```java
System.out.println(3 << 4);    // 48
System.out.println(-16 >> 2);  // -4
System.out.println(-1 >>> 28); // 15
System.out.println(~5);        // -6
```

Gotcha: `>> k` rounds down, but `/` truncates toward zero. They agree on positives and disagree on any negative that 2 to the k does not divide evenly: `-7 >> 1` is -4 while `-7 / 2` is -3.

Gotcha: an int shift uses only the low 5 bits of the distance, so `1 << 32` is 1, not 0. For shifts of 32 or more, shift a long: `1L << 40`.

example.title: Shifting pairs
example.prompt: For each line of n and k, print n << k, n >> k, n / (1 << k), n >>> k, and ~n.
example.explanation: `5 << 2` is 5 times 4. For -7, `>> 1` rounds down to -4 while `/ 2` truncates to -3, so they disagree. For -16 the division is exact, so they agree. `>>>` shifts zeros into the sign bit, which turns both negatives here into large positives. `~n` always equals `-n - 1`: `~5` is -6 and `~-7` is 6.

practice.title: Shift versus divide
practice.prompt:
For each line of n and k, print the three shifts and whether n >> k matches division.

1. Keep reading pairs until input ends (the loop is ready).
2. For each pair print one line `n=N k=K: << A, >> B, >>> C, W`, where A, B, and C are `n << k`, `n >> k`, and `n >>> k`.
3. W is `same` when `n >> k` equals `n / (1 << k)`, otherwise `different`.

Input:

```text
3 4
-9 2
-1 28
```

Expected output:

```text
n=3 k=4: << 48, >> 0, >>> 0, same
n=-9 k=2: << -36, >> -3, >>> 1073741821, different
n=-1 k=28: << -268435456, >> -1, >>> 15, different
```
hints: `1 << k` is 2 to the k, so `n / (1 << k)` divides by it.
Compare `n >> k` with `n / (1 << k)` using `==`. Shifts bind tighter than `==`, so unlike `&` no parentheses are required, but they help readers.

steps.title: Bit masks
steps.body:
A bit mask packs many on/off flags into one int, one flag per bit. Bits count from 0 at the right. Build a one-bit mask with `1 << i`, then combine it with the bit operators `&`, `|`, `^`, and `~`:

- Test bit i: `(n >> i) & 1` is 1 when the bit is on, 0 when it is off.
- Set bit i: `n | (1 << i)` turns it on.
- Clear bit i: `n & ~(1 << i)` turns it off. The `~` makes a mask with every bit on except bit i.
- Toggle bit i: `n ^ (1 << i)` flips it.

```java
int flags = 0b0101;
boolean on = ((flags >> 2) & 1) == 1; // true
flags = flags | (1 << 1);             // 0b0111
flags = flags & ~(1 << 0);            // 0b0110
```

None of these change `n` on their own: they build a new int, so assign it back when you want to keep it. The short forms `|=`, `&=`, and `^=` do that too.

Gotcha: the test gives an int, not a boolean, so compare it with `== 1` before using it in an `if`. Setting a bit that is already on, or clearing one that is already off, changes nothing.

example.title: Permission flags
example.prompt: Read a permissions mask and a bit index, then print whether that bit is set and the mask after setting, clearing, and toggling it.
example.explanation: 13 is 00001101, so bit 2 (the third from the right) is on and the test gives 1. Setting it changes nothing, clearing it removes 4 to give 9, and toggling it also turns it off. Each line builds a new int from `mask`, so `mask` itself never changes.

practice.title: Set one, clear another
practice.prompt:
Read a mask and two bit indexes a and b, report both bits, then set bit a and clear bit b.

1. Print `bit A set: true` or `bit A set: false`, where A is the index a, then the same line for bit b.
2. Set bit a in the mask first, then clear bit b in that result.
3. Print `result: ` followed by the decimal value, a space, and its 8-bit binary.

Input:

```text
9 1 3
```

Expected output:

```text
bit 1 set: false
bit 3 set: true
result: 3 00000011
```

tests.output:
bit 1 set: false
bit 3 set: true
result: 3 00000011

bit 7 set: false
bit 0 set: false
result: 128 10000000

bit 4 set: true
bit 4 set: true
result: 239 11101111

hints: Move bit a down to position 0 with `mask >> a`, then keep only that bit with `& 1` and compare it with 1.
Set with `| (1 << a)` and clear with `& ~(1 << b)`.
Clear after setting, so when a equals b the bit ends up off.

steps.title: Bit tricks

example.title: Find the odd one out
example.prompt: Read numbers until input ends, print for each whether it is a power of two and its bit count, then XOR them all to find the value that appears an odd number of times.
example.output:
8: power of two true, bits 1
6: power of two false, bits 2
0: power of two false, bits 0
1: power of two true, bits 1
6: power of two false, bits 2
8: power of two true, bits 1
0: power of two false, bits 0
odd one out: 1
example.explanation: 1 and 8 have a single 1 bit, so `x & (x - 1)` is 0. Zero gives 0 too, but `x > 0` rules it out. `Integer.bitCount` counts the 1 bits directly. The pairs of 8, 6, and 0 cancel under XOR, which leaves 1 in `odd`.

practice.title: Bit summary
practice.prompt:
Read numbers until input ends and summarize their bits.

1. Count how many numbers are powers of two.
2. Add up the 1 bits of every number.
3. XOR every number together to find the one that appears an odd number of times.
4. Print the three lines the starter already prints.

Input:

```text
3 5 16 3
5 9 9
```

Expected output:

```text
powers of two: 1
one bits: 13
odd one out: 16
```

tests.output:
powers of two: 1
one bits: 13
odd one out: 16

powers of two: 1
one bits: 1
odd one out: 64

powers of two: 0
one bits: 9
odd one out: 7

hints: Use `odd ^= x` so pairs cancel out.

recap:
- `0b1010` is a binary literal. `Integer.toBinaryString` and `Integer.parseInt(s, 2)` convert both ways. Pad with `String.format("%8s", ...).replace(' ', '0')`.
- `&`, `|`, `^`, and `~` work bit by bit. Parenthesize bit tests: `(n & 1) == 0`.
- `<<` multiplies by powers of 2, `>>` keeps the sign and rounds down, `>>>` fills with zeros.
- `~x == -x - 1`. Int shifts use only the low 5 bits of the distance, so use `1L << k` for shifts of 32 or more.
- Masks: test `(n >> i) & 1`, set `n | (1 << i)`, clear `n & ~(1 << i)`, toggle `n ^ (1 << i)`.
- Tricks: `n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0`, `Integer.bitCount`, and XOR of all values finds the odd one out.
